name: PPT: Team development
text: Team development Dr/ Hoda Khalifa Professor of Histology and cell biology Vice dean of students’ affairs Who previously work in teams? What was your role? What did you achieve through this work? Transfer Goal Appreciate being a part of a team and apply teamwork-skills Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this lecture the student will be able to: Describe the stages of team development Analyze the causes of success and failure of the teamwork Outline Definition Importance Requirements Characteristics Stages Success& failure What is a team? A team is a group of people who collaborate on related tasks toward a common goal. Each member is responsible for contributing to the team, but the group as a whole is responsible for the team’s success. What is a teamwork? A set of interdependent activities performed by individuals who collaborate toward a common goal. It involves shared responsibility and collaboration toward a common outcome. Five characteristics of effective teamwork are shared values, mutual trust, inspiring vision, skills, and rewards. Brings new ideas. Helps solving problems Builds morale Gives more learning opportunities Improves sense Of Accomplishment Builds stronger relationships 8 Where can we use teamwork? PBL Group discussion in practical and applied session Group assignment and projects Community visits Working in health team Sport teams Essentials for a team An adequate team size (5-12 members). Presence of a clear and attainable goal. Presence of a team leader. Availability of sufficient resources. Clear roles for everyone in the team. Stages of Team Development Forming Storming Norming Performing Adjourning Forming stage It involves a period of orientation and getting acquainted. Uncertainty is high during this stage, and people are looking for leadership and authority. A member who asserts authority or is knowledgeable may be looked to take control. Team members are asking such questions as “What does the team offer me?” “What is expected of me?” “Will I fit in?” Most interactions are social as members get to know each other. Storming stage It is the most difficult and critical stage to pass through. Marked by conflict and competition as individual personalities emerge. Members may disagree on team goals, and subgroups. Teams can get bogged down in this stage. Failure to address conflicts may result in long-term problems. 13 Norming stage Conflict is resolved and some degree of unity emerges. Consensus develops around who the leader is Individual member’s roles are clear Interpersonal differences begin to be resolved. Sense of cohesion and unity emerges. Performing stage Consensus and cooperation have been well-established The team is mature, organized, and well-functioning. There is a clear and stable structure, and members are committed to the team’s mission. Problems and conflicts still emerge, but they are dealt with constructively. The team is focused on problem solving and meeting team goals. Adjourning stage Most of the team’s goals have been accomplished. The emphasis is on wrapping up final tasks and documenting the effort and results Individual members may be reassigned to other teams, and the team disbands. Ceremonial acknowledgement of the work and success of the team can be helpful. Team Effectiveness Curve Why? What are the causes of success? 1. Communication 2. Delegation 3. Efficiency 4. Ideas 5. Support What are the Benefits of Teamwork for Student? 1. Teaches essential social skills 2. Improves self-confidence 3. Reduces bullying (social media) 4. Sets students up for future success What are the causes of underperformance? Poor communication Ineffective leadership Environmental pressures of disengagement Lack of motivation Lack of formal training Barriers to group effectiveness No clear sense of purpose& goals Unequal member participation Poor listening skills Lack of openness and healthy conflict; expression and idea exchange Lack of trust and communication; fear of reprisal Barriers to group effectiveness Ineffective leadership Lack of motivation Lack of formal training Lack of resources Presence of groupthink What is the groupthink? Is it good or bad? Groupthink is an unhealthy decision-making pattern characterized by a high degree of cohesiveness and a striving for consensus among the members of a decision-making group. Janis and Mann (1977) Symptoms of Groupthink Rationalization Unquestioned beliefs in the group’s morality Stereotyped views of opponents An illusion of invulnerability Symptoms of Groupthink Peer pressure and self-appointed protectors against adverse information Self-censorship and unanimity Mindguards Decision-making results obtained from groupthink situations usually: Include few alternatives Have little or no reexamination of preferred or rejected alternatives Are a selective bias of new information, lacking any contingency plan Groups with moderate cohesiveness produce better decisions than either low or highly cohesive groups. Why? Self-Justification Social Loafing Group-Serving/Self-Serving Bias Conformity Diversity influences within the group Highly cohesive groups suffer from: How to improve your teamwork skills? Get honest feedback. Set personal goals. . Practice. Mimic others with strong teamwork skills. . Resources: https://courses.lumenlearning.com https://www.deakinco.com/resource/the-five-elements-of-successful-teamwork https://www.marlborough.org/ https://www.fmlink.com/articles/barriers-group-effectiveness/ https://www.predictiveindex.com/blog/reasons-teams-underperform/ https://allthingstalent.org/2019/04/16/why-teams-fail-prevent-it 34

text: Introduction to Reflection Presented by: Dr/ Hoda Khalifa Professor of Histology and cell biology Vice dean of students’ affairs Prepared by: Dr. Noha Mahmoud PhD in Medical Education Lecturer of Medical Education Dear students & Transfer Goal You will integrate reflection in your personal and professional practices. What is reflection ? What does reflection mean to you ? ask participants to take three minutes to ask participants what reflective practice means to them, ask them to write their thoughts down and share in large groups 11 REFLECTION REFL -ACTION Thinking about and learning from past experiences to avoid things that did not work and to repeat things that did Active, persistent, and careful consideration of thoughts and beliefs Did we encounter reflection before ? 15 Go around and ask them about their least favorite type of food Ask them about the experience of tasting it for the first time Ask them what they feel hen they see this type of food and how the interact 16 Why ? Why do we reflect ? f you know what worked then you can repeat this in the future  Gives you areas for improvement/development  Aid creativity and helps to avoid stagnation  Helps to overcome assumptions we might make about other people  Key part of emotional intelligence  Helps to maintain a healthy work/life balance 18 Slow down thinking process Reexamine our thoughts, feelings and belief Learning from experience Self Others It is time to ask your questions now ☺ Can we reflect on every moment in our personal and professional life? When to reflect? About what we learn in different classes or readings About an experience we had it may have made you question an aspect of your beliefs, values, attitude or behavior. Incorporate methods of active learning in their educational practice. Outline Part 1: Active learning: What, Why, How? Part 2: Examples of Active Learning Part 3: Pros and Cons Part 4: Let’s play! Q: What is active learning? What is active learning? “An approach to instruction that involves actively engaging students with the course material through discussions, problem solving, case studies, role plays and other methods.” What is active learning? Active learning is: - Student-centered - Students are active parts in the learning process - Instructor is a facilitator What is active learning? Why active learning? Active learning helps students to become lifelong learners. Active learning encourages success. Active learning is engaging and intellectually exciting. How to achieve active learning? How to achieve active learning? The Pause Procedure 2-Minute Activity Think in pairs: what are some examples of active learning? How to achieve active learning? Learning the information within its context. You learn from trial and error. Free thinking and creativity are encouraged. Collaborative learning is encouraged. Time consuming. Students could develop misconception Not all outcomes are predictable Summary or take-home message Active learning is an approach to actively engage students in the learning process. In active learning, students and learning are the center of the education process. Methods of active learning are numerous and range from simple to complex ones. name: PPT: Assessment in medical school
text: Assessment in medical school Dr/ Hoda Khalifa Professor of Histology and cell biology Vice dean of students’ affairs Transfer Goal Understand the Academy College of Medicine’s assessment system. Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this lecture the student will be able to: Discuss types of assessment Correlate assessment methods with different ILO’s Outline What is assessment? Why? When (exam schedule)? How (types of exams)? Grading & Regulation What is assessment? The process of documenting, usually in measurable terms, knowledge, skills, attitudes and beliefs. For the students: Achieving the learning objectives Measuring performance Diagnosing students ’ problems Measuring improvement Selecting (ranking) individuals Why? Types of Exams: 1- Formative Assessment 2- Summative Assessment When? Formative with no summative results Foster development &improvement Summative Results evaluation focus on the outcome Formative Assessment Assessment of efforts prior to their completion for improvement. Formative evaluation is not an end in itself. How to do formative assessment? Pre-reading quiz The one-minute paper Think-pair-share Practical quiz Multiple choice question Problem-based learning (PBL) When? Summative Exams Continuous assessment: Represents 30% Assignment: Represents 10% Practical exam: Represents 20% Final written exams: Represents 40% At the end of each course 11 What do we assess? We assess students to find out if they have acquired the expected knowledge, skills, and attitudes. Competencies ?? Knowledge and Understanding Intellectual Skills Clinical, Procedural, Practical and Technical Skills Professional Attitude and Behavioral Skills Communication Skills General and Transferable Skills Competency includes: Institutional Mission Course Contents Teaching/ Learning Methods Assessment methods Course SLOs Intended learning outcomes: Knowledge and Understanding Intellectual (Application, Problem Solving and Decision Making) Skills Practical (Clinical, Procedural and Technical) skills Professional Ethics/Attitudes and Behavioral Skills Communication Skills General and Transferable Skills Written OSPE & OSCE Assignment Portfolio How? Alignment with the ILO’s Summative Assessment Summative Assessment Written Practical/ clinical projects& Assignment Knowledge levels Problem solving Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) Extended Matching Questions Objective written exams Lead-in (question) Alternatives (options or choices): One correct answer, and several wrong distractors. How MCQ items are constructed? Did you use it before? Extended Matching Questions it must follow a theme: Built upon a theme: 1- An option list (Generally more than 5, usually 8) 2- A lead-in statement 3- Three or four stems or clinical scenarios. 4- For each stem, the candidate should choose the most appropriate option from A–H. 5- If an option will be correct for more than one question, there must be a written instruction. How EMQ (Extended Matching Questions) are constructed? 22 Extended Matching Q Lead in Scenarios or Q Integrated questions At the end of each course Is there Essay Questions? Not in the pre- clerkship phase But short answer questions will be used Constructed around a patient scenario. The questions are revealed in a sequential manner Resembles real-life. Designed to test problem solving and decision making ability of students. In clerkship phase Modified essay questions MEQ How do professional skills be examined? 31 32 OBJECTIVE STRUCTURED PRACTICAL EXAMINATION (OSPE) What is in the stations? Stationary Station ... : Show the Ulnar Nerve in the anatomical specimen Dynamic Station ... : Examine the provided urine sample for proteins Check list will be prepared for dynamic stations 35 ? Station ...: Measure the weight of ( yourself / colleague etc … ? Station ...: Interpret the effect of continuous stimulation on the muscle twitch curve 37 OBJECTIVE STRUCTURED CLINICAL EXAMINATION (OSCE) Characteristics of the OSCE In most stations students are observed (by one or more examiners) Scored as they carry out the task or interpret clinical materials (e.g. laboratory data, X-rays), write notes or answer question Exam Venue How does stations’ exchange occur? All program required elective courses. The Portfolio evaluation. Elective courses marks for are not counted in the graduation cumulative marks Honours تمنح مرتبة الشرف للطالب الذي لا يقل معدله التراكمي عن 3.00 مع تحقيق مثل هذا المعدل على الأقل خلال جميع فصول الدراسة وأن لا يكون حصل علي تقدير F في أي مقرر خلال درا سته منح مرتبة الشرف Violations of exams regulations and academic integrity Disobeying examination instructions Disrupting the discipline or quietness of the exam hall. For example: - Repeated talking. - Repeated showing a switched off mobile during the exam. - Repeated ringing of a mobile phone. oral warning for the first time only, then student is dismissed from the exam and allocated “zero”. Refusing to carry out instructions Repetition of any of the offenses mentioned in item number (1) in any other subject during the exam period. The student is dismissed from the examination hall and the grade allocated to the subject is “F”. Violations of exams regulations and academic integrity Cheating Using any cheating methods. For example: - A switched-on mobile phone that contains course information. - An unauthorized paper slip, table, notes or any other means or tools with course information. - Exchanging answer or questions sheet with a colleague during the exam. - Exchanging tools with information about the subject with a colleague during the exam. - Failing to observe the required regulations for academic integrity. The student fails the subject in question. The grades allocated to the two subsequent subjects (or the two previous ones) should be “W”. Violations of exams regulations and academic integrity Offending the invigilator or the exam supervision authority verbally or physically. Offending the invigilator or the exam supervision authority whether verbally or physically. - The student fails all courses registered for this semester (all subjects “F”). - The student’s registration for the following semester will be suspended. The case is then forwarded to the Student Affairs Committee to determine whether the student is to continue his/her studies at the Academy or not. Impersonation of another student to sit for the exam instead of him/her. Final expulsion from the Academy. name: PPT: Introduction to healthcare system
text: Introduction to healthcare system Dr/ Hoda Khalifa Professor of Histology and cell biology Vice dean of students’ affairs Transfer Goal Be oriented with the healthcare system and his future role as a physician. What do you want to know about health& the healthcare system in Egypt? Hospitals of Health Insurance- Military Hospitals 1ry, 2ry & 3ry healthcare Ambulatory- stationary Hospitals of Ministry Of Health& High Education Health- disease Outpatient- inpatient Governmental - private MS or MD Egyptian Fellowship, Arab Board Of Doctors& others Students’ learning outcomes At the end of this lecture the student will be able to: Discuss health dimensions Classify the health care services according to level, site, patients’ stay, rapidity and finance Identify his road to be specialist Outline What is health and its dimensions? What are the levels of health care What are the elements of primary health care? How to be a specialist? What is inpatient and outpatient medical services? How can the patient choose a hospital? Do you know such terms? Health promotion: The process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health. Health education: One of the measure of health promotion directed towards personal hygiene, nutrition, life style adopted by individual/ group of people by him self or themselves Health counselling: Any assistance to an individual seeking to solve any health problem Dimensions of Health Health care services Level Financial Site Rapidity stay payment Fund 3ry Inpatient Outpatient Medical center Hospital 2ry 1ry Center of Excellence Polyclinic Clinic Governmental private Ministry of Health High education Interior and Defense Urgent Emergency Rapid Semi- elective Elective Levels of Healthcare Primary care General practitioner Secondary care is the care of a specialist. Tertiary care is a higher level of specialized care within a hospital. Primary Healthcare: The primary focus is on the basic healthcare services that address the health issues faced by an individual. The care is mostly provided by a general physician, and they do not require a specialist Needs: Illness: When you notice a new symptom or infection. Injury: acute medical problem. Referral: to specialists and other levels of care. Who can offer this service? Doctors. Nurse practitioners Physician assistants Nutrition vaccination Maternal & child health Infectious disease prevention & treatment Endemic disease treatment Drug availability Health education & counselling Elements of Primary health care Providers Secondary Healthcare: Specialists The providers act as a channel of communication for a better advanced medical care. Specialists focus either on a specific system of the body or a particular disease as: Cardiologists focus on the heart and blood vessels. Endocrinologists focus on hormone systems, including diseases like diabetes and thyroid disease. Oncologists specialize in treating cancers, and many focus on a specific type of cancer. Tertiary Care and Hospitalization It requires highly specialized equipment and expertise as advanced diagnostic centers, specialized intensive care units and modern medical. It is the site for specialized procedures such as: Coronary artery bypass surgery Plastic & Neurosurgeries Severe burn treatments Complex treatments or procedures 17 Who can provide the service? Earning Bachelor of Medicine and Surgery , MBBCH (GP: General Practitioner) Completing training & earning Licensing Residency& advances studies Earning advanced certification (Specialist) How to Become a specialist in Egypt? Egyptian Fellowship MCCQE. Earning Bachelor of Medicine and Surgery , MBBCH (GP: General Practitioner) Completing training & earning Licensing Residency& advances studies Earning advanced certification (Specialist) MS& MD Arab Board of Medical Specializations USMLE PLAB Patients’ stay What is outpatient care? The patient don’t have to stay in a hospital. Outpatient care may be provided in a hospital, as well as a walk-in clinic, an outpatient surgery center, and even the doctor’s office. 22 What are the types of outpatient care? Medical screenings such as mammogram, colonoscopy, and endoscopy Minor surgeries and procedures that don’t require advanced medical care, such as laser surgery, hand or foot surgery, mole removal, and Lasik eye surgery Certain types of treatment used for ongoing or long-term illnesses, such as dialysis and chemotherapy What is inpatient care? provided in a hospital or other type of inpatient facility, where the patient is admitted, and spend at least one night—or more—depending on his condition. The patient is under the care of doctors, nurses, and other types of health care professionals within a hospital. Inpatient stay may be planned or unplanned. What are the examples of inpatient care? Serious illness, such as stroke, heart attack Traumatic injury Severe burns Serious mental health issues, and overdoses Chronic diseases, such as cancer requiring specialized treatment and ongoing care Site of health care delivery Clinic Mono disciplinary Polyclinic Could be integrated with different specialties Medical Center Could be integrated with different specialties Inpatient& Short term Hospital Integrated with different specialties Inpatient & Long term Center of excellence Highly specialized , integrated with different specialties Inpatient & Long term Hospitals& Governance University hospitals, Research institutes Hospitals of Ministry of health Health Insurance hospitals Military hospitals Private hospitals Hospitals& Governance University hospitals, Research institutes Ministry of Higher Education Hospitals of Ministry of health Ministry of Health and Population Health insurance hospitals Health Insurance Organization Military hospitals Ministries of Interior and Defense Patients have the liberty of choosing their doctor based on their financial abilities Private Healthcare Private insurance options and a network of private healthcare providers. Profit clinics, hospitals, and pharmacies The private medical sector is believed to be superior to the public services, in terms of quality. Assess outcomes and competencies where other tools have been less successful Evidence collected over a period of time Group of quantitative & qualitative evidence An overall & holistic view of student’s competence Learner centered and learner involvement Powerful tool for both learning & assessment – focuses student’s attention on the LOs expected and integrates learning & assessment Healthcare provider Health promoter Professional Scholar & scientist Member of healthcare team Lifelong learner & researcher What is a Portfolio? “A collection of work carried out over a period of time as an evidence demonstrating that learning has taken place. Patients’ expectations of individual physicians and of medicine are well documented. They want accessible care within the context of a health care system that is value-laden, equitable, and adequately funded and staffed. They want their physicians to be competent, caring, and compassionate, to listen to them, to be accountable, and to demonstrate qualities that lead to trust. They want to be able to preserve their own dignity and autonomy in decision making. Finally, they want some input into public policy. Government expectations, although less explicitly documented, are made known. They make assumptions upon which public policy is grounded, and these assumptions serve as the basis of their expectations of medicine (Le Grand, 2003). As long as the privilege of self- 34 SOCIETY PHYSICIANS Let us write contract Patients’ expectations of individual physicians and of medicine are well documented. They want accessible care within the context of a health care system that is value-laden, equitable, and adequately funded and staffed. They want their physicians to be competent, caring, and compassionate, to listen to them, to be accountable, and to demonstrate qualities that lead to trust. They want to be able to preserve their own dignity and autonomy in decision making. Finally, they want some input into public policy. Government expectations, although less explicitly documented, are made known. They make assumptions upon which public policy is grounded, and these assumptions serve as the basis of their expectations of medicine (Le Grand, 2003). As long as the privilege of self-regulation is granted to the medical profession, they expect the profession to assure the competence of its members. They require compliance with laws related to health care and also expect that members of the medical profession will be trustworthy. They believe that professions should serve as a source of objective advice—even if this advice is often ignored—and they believe that because of the privileged position of the medical profession, the profession and its members must be devoted to the public good. Finally, they require new levels of accountability (Wynia et al., 1999) and want the profession to practice team health care, expectations that have become much more important in recent times. 35 Arab Academy for Science, Technology & Maritime Transport Faculty of Medicine Program specification of Undergraduate Medical Education Program Reference All the pictures included in presentation were obtained from google search Cruess SR. text: CHEMICAL BLOCKS OF LIFE: LIPIDS By Dr Sara Assem Lecturer of Medical Biochemistry & Molecular Biology DEAR STUDENTS & TRANSFER GOAL Understand the nature and importance of lipids as main nutrients and building block. STUDENTS’ LEARNING OUTCOMES(SLOs) At the end of this session, the student will be able to: Describe how lipids help us function and survive Describe the building blocks of lipids Discuss lipids’ role in health and disease Antibodies Lipids WHAT ARE LIPIDS? Heterogeneous organic compounds related to fatty acids. They contain C, H, and O and may also contain P, N, and S. Lipids are relatively insoluble in water, and soluble in in nonpolar solvents (fat solvents) as ether, benzene and acetone. These molecules are highly water insoluble and must be transported in the circulation in association with protein. 1- Amphipathic 2- FATTY ACID SATURATION In general, addition of double bonds decreases the melting temperature (Tm) of a fatty acid, whereas increasing the chain length increases the Tm In humans, the majority are saturated or monounsaturated. 3 carbons apart 2- FATTY ACID SATURATION In general, addition of double bonds decreases the melting temperature (Tm) of a fatty acid, whereas increasing the chain length increases the Tm Cis Bonds Trans Bonds functional group on the same side functional group on opposite sides 3- FATTY ACID CHAIN LENGTH Short Chain FA 2-6 carbons Medium Chain FA 7-12 carbons Long Chain FA >12 Play role in intestinal health They are now gaining popularity as a healthy diet component and as a dietary supplement where it contains fewer calories and gives higher satiety . Moreover, they improve gut health by killing harmful bacteria without impacting good bacteria, preventing diarrhea and bloating. They are the greatest bulk of FA in animal tissues and most animal diets. In the human body, fatty acids with an even number of carbon atoms (16, 18, or 20) predominate. Longer fatty acids (>22 carbons) being found in the brain. 4-RANCIDITY Slight hydrolysis of fat leading to liberation of short chain FA volatile having bad odour Oxidation of the unsaturated fatty acids occurs with the formation of peroxides, aldehydes and ketones RANCIDITY Can be inhibited by keeping fat in cold clean place away from light and moisture or addition of antioxidant like vitamins A, E. 5-FATTY ACIDS NUMBERING There are two systems of numbering the carbon atoms in a fatty acid ESSENTIAL FA THAT MUST BE PROVIDED IN DIET INCLUDE: Linoleic acid, the precursor of ω-6 fatty acids (ie: Fatty acids with the terminal double bond being six bonds from the ω end.) α-linolenic acid, the precursor of ω-3 fatty acids. (ie: Fatty acids with the terminal double bond being three bonds from the ω end.) Essential fatty acid deficiency occurs most often in infants fed diets deficient in EFAs. Hair loss, low platelets and intellectual disability. Dietary replenishment of EFAs reverses the deficiency. What is the importance of Lipids in Human Body? Structural elements in biological membranes Store and supply energy with 1 gram of dietary lipids providing about 9 Cal . As signalling molecules in cellular response pathways Transport of fat-soluble vitamins Disruption of their levels due to increased dietary intake or abnormal metabolism by the body Related to many diseases including obesity,diabetes, atherosclerosis and abnormalities in fat-soluble vitamin. text: Basics of writing essay & reflections SLO’s At the end of this session the students will be able to Conclude the requirements for medical academic writing. Identify common forms of medical academic writing (such as essays, lab reports, case studies and journal articles). Apply text referencing and avoid plagiarism Outline the needs for reflective writing Apply the principals of the medical academic writing versus reflective writing Take few minutes then decide Look at the following text extract, Is it a sample of academic writing? Stress and its correlates among medical students in six medical colleges: an attempt to understand the current situation Abstract Background: Medical students encounter various stressors during their studies. The study aimed to assess stress levels, sources, and associated determinants among Sudanese medical students. Method: An online questionnaire-based study was conducted among 617 undergraduate medical students of 6 different universities in Sudan. A 19-item questionnaire was utilized to assess stress sources, in addition to demographics, stress manifestations, and coping strategies. Results: The overall prevalence of stress was 31.7% (p <0.05). The main sources of stress were time pressure, heavy workload, fear of failure, and examination frequency. One-third of students indicated that they experienced at least one source of psychosocial- and teaching-related stress. Female medical students were more significantly stressed due to academics than males. Also, fourth- and fifth-year students were academically more stressed in comparison to the first-year students. Poisson regression analysis model showed that first-year students were less stressed than the final-year students in relation to academics (odds=0.888, P=0.003). Male medical students, across all study years, were far less stressed than females (odds=0.901, P=0.000153). Expectedly, ‘studying medicine by choice’ was associated with decreased odds for psychosocial stressors (odds=0.885, P=0.00781), and improved model-fit (chi squared=6.8952, P=0.008643). Also, the year of study was a predictor of teaching-related stress development Conclusions: Female medical students were more stressed due to academics than males. On the other hand, final year students were more academically stressed than first-year students. Female medical students were likely having stress related to academic stress development, while being first-year medical student was a predictor of not developing academic stress. Studying medicine by choice’ was associated with ability to cope against stress. Keywords: Stress, Medical students, Medical education, Sudan It is an example of Academic writing. What in fact are the characteristics that lead us to this conclusion? What linguistic features and other characteristics in your opinion make this an example of medical academic writing? What is academic writing? Based on facts and data (research, not opinions) Sounds formal (uses an academic vocabulary) Draws on information from expert sources (references) Based on facts and data Source: research work with reference we use other people’s information, and show respect to those who wrote it It is written in a formal-sounding vocabulary (which uses academic words and avoids the personal perspective) We use other people’s information, and show respect to those who wrote it Do you really write like that? Really no one writes like this EXCEPT in academic writing When you will use academic writing? To present an assignment (poster, article or power point presentation) To share in students’ conferences To share in scientific competitions Academic writing – general rules The use of sources Quotations Vocabulary characteristic of a specific field Formal language and format Vocabulary Structures Absence of features of spoken language Layout Matter-of-fact style Style of academic writing Formal Impersonal Precise Cautious Unemotional Style of academic writing Formality This piece of writing 🡪the present study (=this study) My essay’ ll make it clear 🡪the present paper will clarify • Impersonality Many of my friends and colleagues say that… 🡪 It is commonly said that… I, you, my friend Dave 🡪 the present study/author, one, Robertson (1992) • Precision Pets like cats, dogs, etc. 🡪 pets, such as cats and dogs, Around half of the group 🡪 approximately 53% of the group Style of academic writing • Caution Our study proves that 🡪 This study shows that I’m sure this is so. 🡪 There is reason to believe that this is so. We really couldn’t make anything of the results. 🡪 There were difficulties in analysing the results. • Lack of emotion (an objective, unemotional stance) I think that this idea sucks. 🡪This idea may not be accurate. In my opinion this is a wonderful topic. 🡪This topic is worth investigating because…. Organization Make your texts well-organized: divide your text into sensible components (main sections, paragraphs subsections,.......). What is a paragraph? A paragraph is a collection of related sentences dealing with a single topic. Paragraph style Effective paragraphs = Unity, Coherence &Economy of expression Unity A topic sentence (general idea) Adequate Development (discussed fully and adequately). Cohesion (language indicates the links between the various issues Coherence (interrelated issues are presented logically) Economy of expression Did I do it well? Sorry but there is plagiarism Plagiarism is: (a) a dangerous disease (b) an academic offence (c) an academic website Plagiarism Copied writing from someone else’s work (a book, a website, another student’s essay etc) Used ideas that someone else researched or developed without referencing the original source Made mistakes with their paraphrasing and referencing (such as only putting some parts of the writing into their own words) Paraphrasing means putting ideas into your own words (but you still reference where it came from!) To avoid plagiarism, follow these steps: Take notes when reading: Always take note of where information has come from (where you read it, who wrote it) Develop your skills: Learn how to quote, paraphrase and reference properly Protect yourself: Never give your work/ assignments to another student Types of academic medical writing Essays Reports Lab report Annotated bibliography Case study What Is a Reflective Essay? Analyzing one’s experience, its meaning, and lessons can be learned from it. An experience you will never forget. The moment you overcame a fear. The most difficult choice you had to make. A time your beliefs were challenged. A time something changed your life. A time you felt lost. An introspective look at your choices A moment in your life you would like to relive. A reflective essay It is a type of writing in which you describe some moment or experience from your life or share your thoughts on some text. The experience should explore your personal ideas, feelings, and opinions about the event and how it affected you There is no right or wrong way to write reflectively! Reflective style Personal in nature: use the personal pronoun “I” Talk about your own thoughts and feelings. Not to be too casual or conversational. Include essential details, Written directly and concisely. Clear examples are very useful. Deeper level reflective writing may also connect with the literature as evidence. Howatson-Jones, L (2010). Reflecting writing. In Reflective practice in nursing. Exeter; Learning Matters p. 120-121 Take home message Academic writing: Based on facts and data (research, not opinions) Sounds formal (uses an academic vocabulary) Draws on information from expert sources (references) To avoid plagiarism learn how to quote, paraphrase and reference properly Reflective writing is personal and feelings are the core of it Reference All the pictures included in presentation were obtained from google search https://slideplayer.com/slide/12710164 Cottrell S. name: PPT: Study skills
text: How to study and take exams professionally SLO’s Appraise remembering vs understanding in light of types of memories Apply needed strategies to consolidate the learned knowledge Apply principals of time manage Demonstrate ability to ovoid procrastination Apply strategies for exam taking A doctor’s path Bachelor’s Certification Master Fellowship Board ± Diploma PhD Renewal Memory Declarative Episodic Semantic Non-declarative Procedural Episodic memory Semantic memory Procedural memory Remembering vs understanding Episodic Semantic procedural Learning Related to the theories of conditioning by Ivan Pavlov and B.F. Skinner Has to do more with behaviors, attitudes, and emotions You “learn” to Worry less about exams Be more positive towards studying Focus more during lectures and studying Attend lectures more often أيوة سمعتك، أعمل ايه بقى؟ Phase 1: Pre-lecture prep Before the lecture Playful reading Not looking to remember, learn, or understand Just collect as much random points about the topis so you can join the conversation in the lecture Looking on random sources including non-scientific ones can be useful. This helps you ask your professor about common misconceptions and get an expert rebuttal. Phase 2: Lecture Attentive listening Not looking to remember or learn Very important to UNDERSTAND Take notes about unclear topics, incomplete answers, parts that challenged you, good mind maps, mnemonics….etc Ask a lot of questions DO NOT GO OUT OF THE LECTURE WITH ANY BLURRED POINTS You don’t have to remember everything, but you must understand as much as you can. Phase 3: Review Soon after the lecture Write your own study notes using your lecture notes, textbook, online resources, personal thoughts…etc Integrate information together Integrate with other lectures and topics Find points of concordance and conflict between different fields and topics Phase 4: Consolidation Checkpoints (commonly every 1-2 weeks) Review the material Clarify any missing points by visiting textbooks or other resources and by discussing these specific points with colleagues or professors Phase 5: Revision Immediately before exam Easiest step in studying Refresh your memory by skimming over the large bullet points Practice with questions Rephrase bullet-points into answers Time Management The art of arranging, organizing, scheduling, and budgeting one’s time " Preventing time robberies Social media Video games Computer& calls Time-robbing visitors Attending unorganized meetings Following unclear directions to any place Sleep Stay focused and Don't forget to live your life, enjoy your time and practice your hobbies Procrastination 80%–95% of college students engage in procrastination, planning fallacy, we underestimate the time required to accomplish assignments. "Student syndrome" a student will only begin to fully apply themselves to a task immediately before a deadline. Procrastination Signs: Ø often end up doing something you like to do instead of what you should do. Ø put required work out of sight so you won’t be reminded of it. Ø You tell yourself you need time to relax and rest. Ø You think you are ill Ø You manage to start late and then convince yourself that there isn’t enough time to do the task that day. Ø You conveniently forget to have needed materials at hand to do a task. The act of postponing, delaying or putting off Reactions to procrastination Avoidance& Distraction Trivialization & Denial Downward counterfactuals Humor & Reframing External attributions 22 How to Beat procrastination? 1- Stop thinking. Start doing. 2. Don’t blow a task out of proportion. 3. Just take the first step. 4. Start with the hardest task of your day. 5. Just make a decision. Any decision. 6. Face your fear. 7. Finish it. Exam taken strategies MCQ exams MCQ questions can generally be classified into questions where you: know the answer even before reading the choices need to read the choices to identify the answer will need to think between two close answers Figure out the correct answer by exclusion Without being sure, chose the answer you think makes most sense Have no idea what the right answer is You need to be wary of the effect of anxiety on your performance. Being anxious can affect your memory, attention, concentration, self-confidence, and in general can very easily move questions down several categories. Thus, a question where you could’ve identified the answer easily will suddenly (with self-doubt) become a question where you’re trying to figure the answer out by exclusion. This ends up consuming more time and propagating anxiety causing a vicious cycle and destroying performance MCQ exams MCQ exams Go through the exam answering only questions in the first two categories: know the answer even before reading the choices need to read the choices to identify the answer If you have studied well, this should cover at least 50 – 60% of the questions Next, you go through the remaining questions answering the following two categories: will need to think between two close answers Figure out the correct answer by exclusion This will cover another 20 – 30%. You have now covered 70 – 90% of the exam Finally read the remaining difficult questions from the last two categories well Without being sure, chose the answer you think makes most sense Have no idea what the right answer is At this point, not knowing the answer to these questions may frustrate you but remember you have already finished about 80% of your exam. So, you probably won’t be anxious and even if you are, it’s safe to panic now ☺ Start reading each question and doing your best at figuring the best هبدة you can come up with. If you REALLY draw a blank, then chose one fixed answer for all remaining questions. MCQ exams Essay questions Although mostly outdated, yet long essay questions may still come up in your careers especially in post graduate and oral exams. The proper technique for writing an academic essay is similar to general rules of essay writing everywhere. You have to divide your answer into Opening paragraph, where you rephrase the question and give a present the bullet-points of your answer Several paragraphs detailing key points of your answer (one point/paragraph) End your essay with a review of the points to cover and a conclusion. Presentations Same as essay structure Make use of AV aids. Leave the writing for the slides and use your narration to enrich presentation If you only read words from slides then you might as well have just sent an essay Practical exams “Practical” comes from “practice” Practice, practice, practice Then keep practicing And when done, practice some more When you stop practicing, your “practical” skills will decline If you want to know who in your class is going to get the highest score in practical exams, ask who spent most time practicing. It also helps to understand the reason behind the practice being studied but you really don’t get marks for that, and nothing beats “muscle memory” Summary Types of memories are episodic, semantic and procedural. Good preparation starts before the lecture till the exam. Time management is the art of arranging, organizing, scheduling, and budgeting one’s time. name: PPT: L24: Orientation to cell biology and life cycle
text: Prepared By: Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry & Molecular Biology Orientation to NMD1101 Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Dear students Welcome to NMD1101: “Cell Biology & Life Cycle” Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Basic information you need to know about the course: Code: NMD1101 Credit Hours: 6 No of weeks: 6 Marks: 150 Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology So, what is the goal of studying cell biology and life cycle?? Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology The aim of this course is to help you be acquainted with the structure and function of somatic cells and outline the germ cell division and principals of embryogenesis and fetal progression with respect to genetic outcome. All such topics will be correlated to their impact on health and disease Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology You will be acquainted with: 1- Somatic cells, including all the structures involved in its composition. In addition you will study related molecular and cell biology and their implications in health and disease Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology You will be acquainted with: 2-Germ cells, genetic and principles of embryogenesis and fetal progression with respect to genetic impact in health and disorders. Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology So, what are the basic medical sciences studied along your courses? Anatomy Physiology Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Histology and cell biology Pathology Pharmacology Microbiology/ parasitology Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology 8 So, Can we guide you step by step through this course? Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology All courses studied in the pre-clerkship phase include the following Lectures Practical PBL Tutorials Clinical skills Medical professions Research PBL Lectures Practical 3 41 41 Lectures 11 Practical 3 PBL 6 weeks Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology 10 Cell biology block Important Tips Watch the lectures videos on the youtube channel rather than the portal window. This can allow you to speed up or slow down. You can also turn CAPTIONS ON. Don’t forget to self-correct your activity sheets during face to face sessions Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology Lectures Lectures will be given in hallrooms, with an average of 2 lectures/day. All lectures are given face to face in addition to being recorded on your portal. Practical sessions In the lab Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology In the hall rooms (tutorials) Problem I: The birth of a new drug Problem II: What is Happening to Mr Ahmed? Problem III: Lara’s agony during pregnancy PBL Week 1-6 Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology So, How will I study?? Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology First, check your schedule on daily and weekly basis On the schedule you have on the students’ hub, You will know which lectures you are supposed to prepare for the week You can take advantage of your long weekend to watch these lectures Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology During watching the lectures videos, take notes After the watching the lecture, solve the related activity sheet You can read the PDF before or after watching the lecture If you have any questions after studying, please post them on the discussion forum Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology On your schedule, you will have all lectures “Face To Face”, In face to face sessions, the time will be available for discussions& revising the activity sheets. Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology On your schedule, you also have sessions called “Practical” These practical sessions are intended to be taken in the lab… MAKE SURE YOU HAVE YOUR LAB COATS WITH YOU! In each lecture, the information you are introduced to will be correlated to different health disorders and/or drugs used to modify the condition Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology ASSESSMENT Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology Dr. Yasmine Amr Issa- Associate Professor of Medical Biochemistry andMolecular Biology Assessment Method Weight in marks Periodicity Date Summative Assessment Continuous assessment (week) (30%) 37 Every 2 weeks Cont. assessment 1 MCQs : 4-11-2023 (20 marks) Cont. assessment 2 (short answers): 18-11-2023 (17 marks) Assignment (10%) 15 Once 27-11-2023 Final written (40%) 60 Once 3-12-2023 Practical (20 %) 30 Once 7-12-2023 PBL 8 Assessed along PBL sessions TOTAL MARKS: 150 Formative Assessment In all tutorial and practical classes - Weekly Mock electronic exam - Before each written assessment Mock practical and assignment - Once 25-11-2023 24 The academy teaches through integration.
